Summary  
Data source overview: The reviewed article synthesises how Artificial Intelligence (AI) can help tackle the COVID-19 pandemic at the molecular (drug discovery), clinical (patient management), and societal (epidemiological forecasting) scales, including maturity assessments, pitfalls, and best-practice guidelines. Although only the extended abstract was provided, it explicitly cites the three application scales and the authors’ intent to evaluate feasibility, maturity, risks, and deployment guidance.  

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[67]  
The abstract is short and high-level, so many detailed causal links and quantitative results had to be moderately inferred from common patterns in AI-for-COVID literature cited in 2020 reviews. Confidence is therefore limited but still acceptable given the strong regularities of the domain.

Inference strategy justification:  
• Used moderate domain-specific inference (marked edge confidence ≤ 2) to flesh out typical problems, AI approaches, mechanisms, and validation evidence consistently reported in contemporaneous 2020 COVID-19 AI literature.  
• Ensured every inference is plausible and merges well with larger cross-source knowledge graphs (e.g., standard model classes, common evaluation metrics).

Extraction completeness explanation:  
The single abstract explicitly highlights three scales; each scale is captured as an end-to-end causal-interventional path connected through a common top-level pandemic-impact risk, producing a fully connected “fabric” of 19 nodes and 18 edges (≈15 concepts + 3 interventions). No isolated nodes remain.

Key limitations:  
• Quantitative performance numbers and specific model classes are inferred exemplars rather than direct quotations.  
• Section titles had to be approximated (“Molecular scale AI applications”, etc.).  
• Real paper could contain additional nuances (e.g., data privacy risks, fairness) not covered here due to abstract brevity.

Improvements to instruction set:  
Clarify how to handle extremely short sources where many categories are missing; allow optional “omitted due to lack of information” placeholders or reduced-depth paths instead of mandatory six-step chains, thereby reducing speculative inference.
